claim: Skeletal stem cells (SSCs) have been isolated from periosteum and bone marrow.
source: Skeletal stem cells (SSCs) have been isolated from various tissues, including periosteum and bone marrow, where they exhibit key functions in bone biology and hematopoiesis, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about SSC isolation.

claim: Periosteal SSCs exhibit key functions in bone biology.
source: Skeletal stem cells (SSCs) have been isolated from various tissues, including periosteum and bone marrow, where they exhibit key functions in bone biology and hematopoiesis, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of periosteal SSCs.

claim: Bone marrow SSCs exhibit key functions in hematopoiesis.
source: Skeletal stem cells (SSCs) have been isolated from various tissues, including periosteum and bone marrow, where they exhibit key functions in bone biology and hematopoiesis, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of bone marrow SSCs.

claim: The role of periosteal SSCs in bone regeneration and healing has been extensively studied.
source: The role of periosteal SSCs (P-SSCs) in bone regeneration and healing has been extensively studied, but their ability to contribute to the bone marrow stroma is still under debate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about the state of research.

claim: The ability of periosteal SSCs to contribute to bone marrow stroma is still under debate.
source: The role of periosteal SSCs (P-SSCs) in bone regeneration and healing has been extensively studied, but their ability to contribute to the bone marrow stroma is still under debate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: A mouse whole bone transplantation model mimics initial bone marrow necrosis seen after injury.
source: In the present study, we characterized a mouse whole bone transplantation model that mimics the initial bone marrow necrosis and fatty infiltration seen after injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental model developed in this study.

claim: A mouse whole bone transplantation model mimics fatty infiltration seen after injury.
source: In the present study, we characterized a mouse whole bone transplantation model that mimics the initial bone marrow necrosis and fatty infiltration seen after injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental model developed in this study.

claim: P-SSCs migrate into the bone marrow after transplantation.
source: Using this model and a lineage tracing approach, we observed the migration of P-SSCs into the bone marrow after transplantation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: P-SSCs are phenotypically reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells once in the bone marrow.
source: Once in the bone marrow, P-SSCs are phenotypically and functionally reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) that express high levels of hematopoietic stem cell niche factors such as Cxcl12 and Kitl.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding about P-SSC plasticity.

claim: P-SSCs are functionally reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells once in the bone marrow.
source: Once in the bone marrow, P-SSCs are phenotypically and functionally reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) that express high levels of hematopoietic stem cell niche factors such as Cxcl12 and Kitl.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding about P-SSC plasticity.

claim: Reprogrammed P-SSCs express high levels of Cxcl12.
source: Once in the bone marrow, P-SSCs are phenotypically and functionally reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) that express high levels of hematopoietic stem cell niche factors such as Cxcl12 and Kitl.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding about gene expression changes in P-SSCs.

claim: Reprogrammed P-SSCs express high levels of Kitl.
source: Once in the bone marrow, P-SSCs are phenotypically and functionally reprogrammed into bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) that express high levels of hematopoietic stem cell niche factors such as Cxcl12 and Kitl.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding about gene expression changes in P-SSCs.

claim: P-SSCs are more resistant to acute stress than BM-MSCs.
source: In addition, using ex vivo and in vivo approaches, we found that P-SSCs are more resistant to acute stress than BM-MSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding from stress resistance experiments.

claim: BM-MSCs are rare self-renewing multipotent stromal cells.
source: Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) are rare self-renewing multipotent stromal cells which are capable of multilineage differentiation into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes (Caplan, 1991; Dominici et al., 2006; Frenette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BM-MSCs are capable of multilineage differentiation into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes.
source: Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) are rare self-renewing multipotent stromal cells which are capable of multilineage differentiation into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes (Caplan, 1991; Dominici et al., 2006; Frenette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BM-MSCs are mostly localized around blood vessels.
source: BM-MSCs are mostly localized around the blood vessels and represent an important component of the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) microenvironment, also referred to as the niche.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about BM-MSC localization.

claim: BM-MSCs represent an important component of the hematopoietic stem cell microenvironment.
source: BM-MSCs are mostly localized around the blood vessels and represent an important component of the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) microenvironment, also referred to as the niche.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about BM-MSC function.

claim: BM-MSCs secrete CXCL12 that controls HSC self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation.
source: BM-MSCs closely interact with HSCs and secrete factors, including the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand (CXCL12) and stem cell factor (SCF), that control their self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation capacities (Kunisaki et al., 2013; Asada et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2012; Acar et al., 2015; Omatsu et al., 2010; Sugiyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BM-MSCs secrete SCF that controls HSC self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation.
source: BM-MSCs closely interact with HSCs and secrete factors, including the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand (CXCL12) and stem cell factor (SCF), that control their self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation capacities (Kunisaki et al., 2013; Asada et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2012; Acar et al., 2015; Omatsu et al., 2010; Sugiyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Several studies have used cell surface markers CD51+, PDGFRα+, Sca-1+ to describe distinct BM-MSC populations.
source: Several studies have used cell surface markers (CD51+, PDGFRα+, Sca-1+) or reporter mice (Lepr-cre, Nestin (Nes)-GFP, Ng2-cre) to describe distinct BM-MSC populations with significant overlap (Kunisaki et al., 2013; Asada et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2012; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2014; Pinho et al., 2013; Morikawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The periosteum is a thin layer of fibrous material that covers the surface of long bones.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the periosteum, a thin layer of fibrous material that covers the surface of long bones, is a source of skeletal stem cells (SSCs) for bone regeneration (Chan et al., 2015; Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018; Arnsdorf et al., 2009; Ortinau et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a definition of the periosteum.

claim: The periosteum is a source of skeletal stem cells for bone regeneration.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the periosteum, a thin layer of fibrous material that covers the surface of long bones, is a source of skeletal stem cells (SSCs) for bone regeneration (Chan et al., 2015; Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018; Arnsdorf et al., 2009; Ortinau et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Periosteum SSCs share some characteristics with BM-MSCs.
source: These periosteum SSCs (P-SSCs) have been described as sharing some characteristics with BM-MSCs (Chan et al., 2015; Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The relationship between periosteal SSCs and BM-MSCs is poorly understood.
source: However, the relationship between these different stromal cell populations is poorly understood and the distinction between MSCs and SSCs remains controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The distinction between MSCs and SSCs remains controversial.
source: However, the relationship between these different stromal cell populations is poorly understood and the distinction between MSCs and SSCs remains controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The bone cortex represents a richer source of CFU-F than bone marrow.
source: While the bone marrow is classically known as a major source of MSCs, the bone cortex represents a richer source of colony-forming units-fibroblasts (CFU-F) (Pinho et al., 2013; Mizoguchi et al., 2014; Blashki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Bone regeneration is mediated by both endochondral and intramembranous ossification.
source: It has been suggested that bone regeneration is mediated by both endochondral and intramembranous ossification and that the periosteum plays an important role in bone regeneration after injury (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018; Utvåg et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2017b; Shapiro, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The periosteum plays an important role in bone regeneration after injury.
source: It has been suggested that bone regeneration is mediated by both endochondral and intramembranous ossification and that the periosteum plays an important role in bone regeneration after injury (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018; Utvåg et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2017b; Shapiro, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There is little information on the function of P-SSCs aside from their role in bone healing and remodeling.
source: However, there is little information on the function of P-SSCs, aside from their crucial role in bone healing and remodeling, and whether they contribute to bone marrow regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Cell viability in the graft bone marrow reaches below 10% at 24 hr after transplantation.
source: The bone transplantation is followed by a rapid and massive depletion of bone marrow cells in the engrafted femur with a cell viability reaching below 10% at 24 hr after transplantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing the data.

claim: Bone marrow necrosis following bone transplantation is associated with replacement of hematopoietic cells by marrow adipocytes.
source: Notably, bone marrow necrosis following bone transplantation is associated with the replacement of hematopoietic cells in the graft femur by marrow adipocytes, similar to the effects of chemotherapy or irradiation (Zhou et al., 2017; Yamazaki and Allen, 1991; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and supporting citations.

claim: Bone marrow cellularity progressively increases over time after bone transplantation.
source: Following bone transplantation, we observed a progressive increase in bone marrow cellularity over time with no significant difference in cellularity between the graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: There is no significant difference in bone marrow cellularity between graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation.
source: Following bone transplantation, we observed a progressive increase in bone marrow cellularity over time with no significant difference in cellularity between the graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: Regeneration of the bone marrow compartment is associated with a reduction in adipogenic infiltration.
source: Regeneration of the bone marrow compartment is associated with a reduction in adipogenic infiltration, as revealed by staining with the anti-perilipin antibody at 4-month post-transplantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing the imaging data.

claim: The absolute number of graft BM-MSCs increases over time after bone transplantation.
source: Additionally, the absolute number of graft BM-MSCs, defined as CD45−Ter119−CD31−CD51+CD140α+ cells by flow cytometry (Pinho et al., 2013), also increased over time, with no difference between the graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: There is no difference in BM-MSC numbers between graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation.
source: Additionally, the absolute number of graft BM-MSCs, defined as CD45−Ter119−CD31−CD51+CD140α+ cells by flow cytometry (Pinho et al., 2013), also increased over time, with no difference between the graft and host femurs at 5 months following transplantation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: The number of phenotypic HSCs in the graft femur progressively increases over time.
source: We also observed a progressive increase in the number of Lin−Sca1+cKit+CD48−CD150+ phenotypic HSCs in the graft femur over time (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: The absolute HSC numbers in the graft did not reach HSC numbers in the host femur after 5 months.
source: Although the absolute HSC numbers in the graft did not reach HSC numbers as detected in the host femur after 5 months (Figure 1B), no differences were observed in the numbers of hematopoietic progenitors or in the frequencies of hematopoietic cell populations between the host and graft femurs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: No differences were observed in the numbers of hematopoietic progenitors between host and graft femurs at 5 months.
source: Although the absolute HSC numbers in the graft did not reach HSC numbers as detected in the host femur after 5 months (Figure 1B), no differences were observed in the numbers of hematopoietic progenitors or in the frequencies of hematopoietic cell populations between the host and graft femurs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the data.

claim: No differences were observed in the frequencies of hematopoietic cell populations between host and graft femurs at 5 months.
source: Although the absolute HSC numbers in the graft did not reach HSC numbers as detected in the host femur after 5 months (Figure 1B), no differences were observed in the numbers of hematopoietic progenitors or in the frequencies of hematopoietic cell populations between the host and graft femurs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the data.

claim: 100% of lethally irradiated recipients survived throughout the bone marrow transplantation experiment.
source: The survival of lethally irradiated recipients remained equal in both groups, with 100% of recipients surviving throughout the length of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the bone marrow transplantation assay.

claim: HSCs and progenitors derived from graft femurs can sustain long-term hematopoiesis upon transplantation.
source: Chimerism analysis revealed robust engraftment of recipient mice with hematopoietic cells derived from the engrafted femurs, indicating that HSCs and progenitors derived from graft femurs can sustain long-term hematopoiesis upon transplantation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1D showing the chimerism data.

claim: No significant differences in donor cell contribution to myeloid or lymphoid lineages were observed between graft and host groups.
source: We also observed no significant differences in donor cell contribution to myeloid or lymphoid lineages between the two groups (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1E showing the lineage reconstitution data.

claim: Over 98% of graft BM-MSCs originated from the graft femur at 5 months post-transplantation.
source: Corroborating the results of Picoli et al., 2023, we observed that at 5 months post-transplantation, over 98% of the graft BM-MSCs originated from the graft femur, while over 99% of the hematopoietic cells in the graft originated from the host mouse (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2C and 2D showing the lineage tracing data.

claim: Over 99% of hematopoietic cells in the graft originated from the host mouse at 5 months post-transplantation.
source: Corroborating the results of Picoli et al., 2023, we observed that at 5 months post-transplantation, over 98% of the graft BM-MSCs originated from the graft femur, while over 99% of the hematopoietic cells in the graft originated from the host mouse (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2C and 2D showing the lineage tracing data.

claim: Endothelial cells in the graft were derived from both the host and the graft.
source: Interestingly, endothelial cells were derived from both the host and the graft, suggesting the contribution of different progenitors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: VE-cadherin-labeled vessels are present within the periosteum and crossing the cortical bone of the graft at 15 days and 1 month after transplantation.
source: This revealed the presence of VE-cadherin-labeled vessels within the periosteum and crossing the cortical bone of the graft.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the confocal analysis of VE-cadherin-CreER mice.

claim: Endothelial regeneration occurs at an early stage following bone transplantation.
source: This result demonstrates that endothelial regeneration occurs at an early stage following bone transplantation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the VE-cadherin labeling data.

claim: Both recipient VE-cadherin-labeled and UBC-GFP vessels contribute to the grafted femur at 5 months.
source: Furthermore, when femurs from UBC-GFP mice were transplanted into Cdh5-CreER;iTdTomato mice, contributions of both recipient VE-cadherin-labeled and UBC-GFP vessels were observed 5 months later.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the dual labeling experiment.

claim: No cells derived from the graft were detected in the host femurs.
source: Furthermore, we did not detect any cells derived from the graft in the host femurs (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a negative finding from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Graft Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs show progressive increase in Cxcl12 expression over time, reaching a plateau at 5 months post-transplantation.
source: In addition to the previously described increase over time in the absolute number of BM-MSCs in the graft femur (Figure 1B), we observed a progressive increase in the expression of the HSC-niche genes Cxcl12 and Kitl (which encodes Scf), reaching a plateau at 5-month post-transplantation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2F showing the qPCR data.

claim: Graft Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs show progressive increase in Kitl expression over time, reaching a plateau at 5 months post-transplantation.
source: In addition to the previously described increase over time in the absolute number of BM-MSCs in the graft femur (Figure 1B), we observed a progressive increase in the expression of the HSC-niche genes Cxcl12 and Kitl (which encodes Scf), reaching a plateau at 5-month post-transplantation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2F showing the qPCR data.

claim: No differences were observed between host and graft femurs in expression levels of Opn, Angpt1, and Vcam1 at 5 months.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed between host and graft femurs in the expression levels of additional niche factors, including osteopontin (Opn) (Nilsson et al., 2005; Stier et al., 2005), angiopoietin-1 (Angpt1) (Arai et al., 2004), and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (Vcam1) (Jacobsen et al., 1996; Papayannopoulou et al., 1998) at 5 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and supporting citations.

claim: Host and graft BM-MSCs had similar CFU-F activity at 5 months.
source: In this experiment, host and graft BM-MSCs also had similar CFU-F activity at 5 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2B showing the CFU-F data.

claim: The number of live cells within the bone marrow and compact bone were drastically reduced in the first 24 hr post-transplantation.
source: While the number of live cells within the bone marrow and compact bone were drastically reduced in the first 24 hr post-transplantation, we unexpectedly observed a significant but transient increase in live periosteal cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing the cellularity data.

claim: A significant but transient increase in live periosteal cells was observed in the first 24 hr post-transplantation.
source: While the number of live cells within the bone marrow and compact bone were drastically reduced in the first 24 hr post-transplantation, we unexpectedly observed a significant but transient increase in live periosteal cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing the cellularity data.

claim: Cell viability was not affected in the periosteum shortly after transplantation.
source: Moreover, while most of the bone marrow cells were depleted shortly after transplantation, cell viability was not affected in the periosteum within this time frame (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing the viability data.

claim: CD51+CD200+ P-SSCs had the highest CFU-F activity within the periosteum.
source: Within the CD45−Ter119−CD31− fraction of live periosteal cells, we confirmed that CD51+CD200+ P-SSCs had the highest CFU-F activity and were also capable of trilineage differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E showing the CFU-F and differentiation data.

claim: CD51+CD200+ P-SSCs are capable of trilineage differentiation.
source: Within the CD45−Ter119−CD31− fraction of live periosteal cells, we confirmed that CD51+CD200+ P-SSCs had the highest CFU-F activity and were also capable of trilineage differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E showing the differentiation data.

claim: P-SSCs expand starting at day 3 post-transplantation and peak at day 8.
source: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed an expansion of P-SSCs starting at day 3 post-transplantation and peaking at day 8 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F showing the flow cytometry data.

claim: Nes-GFP+ skeletal progenitors expand within the periosteum with a peak at day 8.
source: We detected an expansion of Nes-GFP+ skeletal progenitors (Tournaire et al., 2020) within the periosteum with a peak at day 8 (Figure 3C), similar to the expansion kinetics that we detected by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C showing the confocal microscopy data and a citation.

claim: Nes-GFP+ cells can be detected outside of the periosteum layer and in the compact bone by day 15.
source: Interestingly, by day 15, we could detect Nes-GFP+ cells outside of the periosteum layer stained by an anti-periostin antibody and in the compact bone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C showing the confocal microscopy data.

claim: Total cellularity and BM-MSC number were significantly reduced in femurs lacking the periosteum at 5 months after transplantation.
source: At 5 months after transplantation, total cellularity and BM-MSC number were significantly reduced in femurs lacking the periosteum, highlighting a potentially critical role for the periosteum and P-SSCs during bone marrow regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the periosteum removal experiment.

claim: P-SSCs were positively enriched for gene sets associated with stemness compared to BM-MSCs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that P-SSCs were positively enriched for gene sets associated with stemness and negatively enriched for gene sets associated with proliferation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A showing the GSEA data.

claim: P-SSCs were negatively enriched for gene sets associated with proliferation compared to BM-MSCs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that P-SSCs were positively enriched for gene sets associated with stemness and negatively enriched for gene sets associated with proliferation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A showing the GSEA data.

claim: P-SSCs express high levels of cell cycle inhibitor genes Cdkn1a and Cdkn1c at steady state.
source: These results are in line with qPCR analysis showing that P-SSCs express high levels of the cell cycle inhibitor genes Cdkn1a and Cdkn1c, and low levels of the cell cycle progression gene Cdk4 at steady state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B showing the qPCR data.

claim: P-SSCs express low levels of cell cycle progression gene Cdk4 at steady state.
source: These results are in line with qPCR analysis showing that P-SSCs express high levels of the cell cycle inhibitor genes Cdkn1a and Cdkn1c, and low levels of the cell cycle progression gene Cdk4 at steady state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B showing the qPCR data.

claim: P-SSCs are less metabolically active than BM-MSCs as shown by decreased glucose uptake.
source: Additionally, flow cytometric analysis revealed that, compared to BM-MSCs, P-SSCs are less metabolically active, as shown by decreased glucose uptake as assessed by 2-(N-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)amino)-2-deoxyglucose (2-NDBG) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4C showing the flow cytometry data.

claim: P-SSCs had lower levels of cellular ROS than BM-MSCs at steady state.
source: At steady state, flow cytometric analysis revealed that P-SSCs had lower levels of cellular ROS than BM-MSCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4D showing the ROS measurement data.

claim: P-SSCs have higher expression of Sod1, Gls, and Gpx1 than BM-MSCs.
source: Indeed, qPCR analysis revealed higher expression of three major ROS-detoxifying enzymes genes: superoxide dismutase (Sod1), glutaminase (Gls) and glutathione peroxidase (Gpx1), in sorted CD51+CD200+ P-SSCs than in CD51+CD200+ BM-MSCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4E showing the qPCR data.

claim: A downregulation of ECM factors such as Fmod and Nid1 occurs in graft P-SSCs as early as 3 days post bone transplantation.
source: As early as 3 days post bone transplantation, we observed a downregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) factors such as fibromodulin (Fmod) and nidogen 1 (Nid1) in the graft P-SCCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing the RNA sequencing data.

claim: Graft P-SSCs show upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication signatures compared to steady-state P-SSCs.
source: Additionally, GSEA comparing steady-state P-SSCs with graft P-SSCs, revealed an upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication signatures and downregulation of ECM–receptor interaction and glutathione metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that a change in the P-SSCs phenotype occurs early after bone transplantation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing the GSEA data.

claim: Graft P-SSCs show downregulation of ECM-receptor interaction and glutathione metabolism compared to steady-state P-SSCs.
source: Additionally, GSEA comparing steady-state P-SSCs with graft P-SSCs, revealed an upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication signatures and downregulation of ECM–receptor interaction and glutathione metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that a change in the P-SSCs phenotype occurs early after bone transplantation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing the GSEA data.

claim: BM-MSCs exhibited a significantly higher level of apoptosis compared to P-SSCs after 12 hr in serum-free media.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of activated caspase-3/7 revealed that after 12 hr in serum-free media, BM-MSCs exhibited a significantly higher level of apoptosis compared to P-SSCs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing the apoptosis data.

claim: P-SSCs are more intrinsically resilient than BM-MSCs when subjected to similar stress conditions in an equivalent environment.
source: These results suggest that P-SSCs are more intrinsically resilient than BM-MSCs, even when they are subjected to similar stress conditions in an equivalent environment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the ex vivo apoptosis assay data.

claim: GFP+ cells from UBC-GFP periosteum are observed within the compact bone at 5 months after transplantation.
source: We then transplanted these bones into WT host mice and observed GFP+ cells within the compact bone at 5 months after transplantation (Figure 5C), consistent with the well-described role of the periosteum in bone remodeling (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018; Julien et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5C and supporting citations.

claim: GFP+ cells from UBC-GFP periosteum enwrap endomucin-stained sinusoids and form a network in the bone marrow.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we also observed GFP+ cells enwrapping endomucin-stained sinusoids and forming a network, similar to the perivascular nature of BM-MSCs (Sugiyama et al., 2006; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2010; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5C and supporting citations.

claim: P-SSCs do not express Cxcl12 or Kitl at steady state.
source: Importantly, while P-SSCs do not express Cxcl12 or Kitl at steady state, periosteum-derived GFP+ BM-MSCs expressed these niche cytokines at a similar level to control sorted Nes-GFP+BM-MSCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5D showing the qPCR data.

claim: Periosteum-derived GFP+ BM-MSCs expressed Cxcl12 and Kitl at a similar level to control sorted Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs.
source: Importantly, while P-SSCs do not express Cxcl12 or Kitl at steady state, periosteum-derived GFP+ BM-MSCs expressed these niche cytokines at a similar level to control sorted Nes-GFP+BM-MSCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5D showing the qPCR data.

claim: Angpt1 expression in graft GFP+ BM-MSCs reached the level of control BM-MSCs at 5 months after transplantation.
source: Similarly, we found that Angpt1 expression in the graft GFP+ BM-MSCs reached the level of control BM-MSCs, while Opn expression was higher in GFP+ BM-MSCs than in control Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs at 5 months after transplantation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing the qPCR data.

claim: Opn expression was higher in graft GFP+ BM-MSCs than in control Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs at 5 months after transplantation.
source: Similarly, we found that Angpt1 expression in the graft GFP+ BM-MSCs reached the level of control BM-MSCs, while Opn expression was higher in GFP+ BM-MSCs than in control Nes-GFP+ BM-MSCs at 5 months after transplantation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing the qPCR data.

claim: Opn is upregulated in settings of inflammation, injury, and migration.
source: However, Opn has been shown to be upregulated in settings of inflammation, injury, and migration (Denhardt et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2017a; Zou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Postn is highly expressed by periosteal cells and upregulated during bone healing and formation.
source: Postn encodes the secreted matricellular protein Periostin, and is highly expressed by periosteal cells and upregulated during bone healing and formation (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Postn is expressed by multiple cell types including osteoblasts and fibroblasts.
source: While Postn is expressed by multiple cell types, including but not limited to osteoblasts and fibroblasts (Horiuchi et al., 1999; Oshima et al., 2002; Oka et al., 2007), its high expression in P-SSCs compared with BM-MSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) makes it a useful marker to distinguish endogenous BM-MSCs from periosteum-derived BM-MSCs after bone transplantation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tomato+ cells are confined to the periosteum and located perivascularly at early time points following bone transplantation.
source: At early time points following bone transplantation, we see Tomato+ cells confined to the periosteum and located perivascularly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the PostnCre-ER lineage tracing experiment.

claim: Tomato+ cells migrate into the bone marrow at 21 days after transplantation.
source: At 21 days after transplantation, we observe Tomato+ cells migrating into the bone marrow (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6B showing the confocal imaging data.

claim: An average of 85.4% of BM-MSCs within the engrafted bone marrow were Tomato+ at 5 months, indicating a periosteal origin.
source: Additionally, flow cytometric analysis revealed that an average of 85.4% (range: 65.0–94.5%) of the BM-MSCs within the engrafted bone marrow were Tomato+, indicating a periosteal origin (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C showing the flow cytometry data.

claim: No difference in P-SSCs expansion or migration into the bone marrow was detected after single limb irradiation.
source: While a clear difference in the architecture of bone marrow vasculature was observed between the non-irradiated and irradiated limbs, no difference in P-SSCs expansion or migration into the bone marrow was detected, contrasting with the findings in our femur transplant model (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2B showing the imaging data.

claim: Bone transplantation results in a more severe injury to the bone marrow compared to localized irradiation.
source: This observation suggests that bone transplantation results in a more severe injury to the bone marrow compared to localized irradiation, thereby enabling the assessment of BM-MSCs' recovery after more severe injury.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the irradiation experiment results.

claim: Periosteum-derived graft BM-MSCs display a gene expression profile distinct from that of both steady-state BM-MSCs and steady-state P-SSCs.
source: Venn diagram and principal component analysis revealed that periosteum-derived graft BM-MSCs display a gene expression profile distinct from that of both steady-state BM-MSCs and steady-state P-SSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B showing the RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: HSC-niche-associated maintenance genes are upregulated in 5-month-old graft BM-MSCs compared to P-SSCs at steady state.
source: Consistent with our previous tracing experiment using UBC-GFP periosteum (Figure 5D), we observed an upregulation of HSC-niche-associated maintenance genes in the 5-month-old graft BM-MSCs compared to P-SSCs at steady state (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6D, E showing the RNA sequencing data.

claim: Postn and other extracellular matrix-related genes such as Fn1 and Fmod are downregulated in periosteum-derived graft BM-MSCs compared with P-SSCs at steady state.
source: We also observed the downregulation of Postn and other extracellular matrix-related genes, such as fibronectin (Fn1) and fibromodulin (Fmod), in periosteum-derived graft BM-MSCs compared with P-SSCs at steady state (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6D, E showing the RNA sequencing data.

claim: P-SSCs can be reprogrammed and adapt a niche-supportive phenotype akin to native BM-MSCs after migrating into the bone marrow following acute stress and subsequent regeneration.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that P-SSCs can be reprogrammed and adapt a niche-supportive phenotype akin to native BM-MSCs after migrating into the bone marrow following acute stress and subsequent regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of the findings.

claim: BM-MSCs play a crucial role in regulating the self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferative properties of HSCs.
source: Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells represent a key component of the bone marrow microenvironment. These stromal cells play a crucial role in regulating the self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferative properties of HSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The periosteum is highly vascularized and innervated.
source: The periosteum, a thin membrane that is highly vascularized and innervated, is located on the outside of the bone.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a description of the periosteum.

claim: The periosteum contains numerous skeletal stromal cells that play a pivotal role in maintaining bone tissue and facilitating post-fracture healing.
source: This membrane contains numerous skeletal stromal cells, which play a pivotal role in maintaining the bone tissue and facilitating post-fracture healing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge about periosteal function.

claim: The mechanisms of bone marrow regeneration and stromal recovery remain poorly understood.
source: While the bone marrow microenvironment at steady state has been extensively studied, the mechanisms of bone marrow regeneration and stromal recovery remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Data related to the functions of P-SSC beyond their established role in bone maintenance and fracture healing remain scarce.
source: Furthermore, data related to the functions of P-SSC beyond their established role in bone maintenance and fracture healing remain scarce.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Prior research has emphasized the significance of stromal integrity for the recovery of HSCs following irradiation or chemotherapy.
source: Prior research has emphasized the significance of stromal integrity for the recovery of HSCs following irradiation or chemotherapy (Banfi et al., 2001; Lucas et al., 2013; Hérodin and Drouet, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: BM-MSCs ultimately demonstrate their capacity to regenerate and sustain hematopoiesis within the engrafted femur.
source: The findings of our study indicate that, while initially impacted by the stress associated with transplantation, BM-MSCs ultimately demonstrate their capacity to regenerate and sustain hematopoiesis within the engrafted femur.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Hematopoietic progenitors derived from the graft femur are capable of engraftment in secondary recipient mice, thereby facilitating multi-lineage reconstitution.
source: Furthermore, our findings indicate that hematopoietic progenitors derived from the graft femur are capable of engraftment in secondary recipient mice, thereby facilitating multi-lineage reconstitution.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: The origin of endothelial progenitors in the bone marrow is not well defined.
source: The origin of endothelial progenitors in the bone marrow is not well defined.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: During bone marrow regeneration after chemotherapy, sinusoidal and arteriolar vessels are derived from distinct progenitors.
source: A recent study showed that during bone marrow regeneration after chemotherapy, sinusoidal and arteriolar vessels are derived from distinct progenitors (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Endothelial regeneration in the graft and vascular anastomoses between the host and graft femur are likely important for the hematopoietic regeneration process.
source: Therefore, it is likely that endothelial regeneration in the graft, and vascular anastomoses between the host and graft femur are also important for the hematopoietic regeneration process.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the study findings.

claim: At steady state, P-SSC do not express HSC maintenance genes such as Kitl and Cxcl12.
source: At steady state, P-SSC do not express HSC maintenance genes, such as Kitl and Cxcl12, and the potential capacity of P-SSC to support HSCs has not been previously addressed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the study.

claim: The potential capacity of P-SSC to support HSCs has not been previously addressed.
source: At steady state, P-SSC do not express HSC maintenance genes, such as Kitl and Cxcl12, and the potential capacity of P-SSC to support HSCs has not been previously addressed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a gap in prior research.

claim: P-SSCs can migrate to the bone marrow and adopt a phenotype similar to that of BM-MSCs.
source: Unexpectedly, our results show that in our model, P-SSCs can migrate to the bone marrow and adopt a phenotype similar to that of BM-MSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a key finding from the study.

claim: P-SSCs can be harvested and manipulated as a source of BM-MSCs.
source: Therefore, it is possible that P-SSCs can be harvested and manipulated as a source of BM-MSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a potential application of the findings.

claim: A recent study employing Gli1 to trace P-SSC demonstrated the localized expression of Kitl and Cxcl12 by P-SSCs at the fracture site.
source: In accordance with our findings, a recent study employing Gli1 to trace P-SSC demonstrated the localized expression of Kitl and Cxcl12 by P-SSCs at the fracture site (Jeffery et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Periostin contributes to the highly regenerative nature of P-SSCs compared to BM-MSCs.
source: Accordingly, Duchamp de Lageneste et al. demonstrated that periostin contributes to the highly regenerative nature of P-SSCs compared to BM-MSCs (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Periostin interacts with extracellular matrix proteins and plays a key role in tissue regeneration and cancer progression.
source: Periostin is a well-studied protein that has been shown to interact with extracellular matrix proteins and plays a key role in tissue regeneration and cancer progression, promoting proliferation, invasion, and anti-apoptotic signaling (González-González and Alonso, 2018; Bao et al., 2004; Butcher et al., 2007; Conway et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: It is possible that periostin contributes to P-SSC proliferation and migration into the bone marrow.
source: Therefore, it is possible that periostin contributes to P-SSC proliferation and migration into the bone marrow, which would be an interesting area for future investigation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation for future research.

claim: BM-MSCs are renowned for their resilience to stress.
source: Additionally, our findings illustrate the differential stress response between BM-MSCs and P-SSCs. While BM-MSCs are renowned for their resilience to stress, our findings illustrate that P-SSCs exhibit an even greater resistance to stress, which is attributed, at least in part, to their distinctive metabolic profile (Morikawa et al., 2009; Haas et al., 1969).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: P-SSCs exhibit an even greater resistance to stress than BM-MSCs, attributed at least in part to their distinctive metabolic profile.
source: Additionally, our findings illustrate the differential stress response between BM-MSCs and P-SSCs. While BM-MSCs are renowned for their resilience to stress, our findings illustrate that P-SSCs exhibit an even greater resistance to stress, which is attributed, at least in part, to their distinctive metabolic profile (Morikawa et al., 2009; Haas et al., 1969).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The observed differences between P-SSCs and BM-MSCs are due to intrinsic cellular properties rather than their anatomical location.
source: Given that differences in apoptosis were observed between BM-MSCs and P-SSCs, even when they were cultured ex vivo under identical stress culture conditions with identical oxygen tension, it can be concluded that the observed differences between P-SSCs and BM-MSCs are due to intrinsic cellular properties rather than their anatomical location.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the ex vivo experiments.

claim: Through their high level of resilience and plasticity, P-SSCs can facilitate BM-MSC regeneration.
source: In conclusion, we have used a whole bone transplantation model to study bone marrow regeneration in vivo in response to acute injury using genetic tools. Our study has shown that through their high level of resilience and plasticity, P-SSCs can facilitate BM-MSC regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study's main conclusion.

claim: P-SSCs are able to contribute to hematopoietic cell recovery under stress conditions.
source: Our data suggest that P-SSCs are able to contribute to hematopoietic cell recovery under stress conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study findings.
